title: Why the same energy shock can deliver a different inflation outcome
summary: At a conference in Rome on 19 November, Banca d’Italia Deputy Governor Sergio Nicoletti Altimari explained why the euro area’s renewed energy shock had so far spread less widely through consumer prices than in 2021–22. Energy-related goods accounted for most of the increase in inflation, while the frequency with which firms changed prices had yet to rise in the microdata he cited. Those observations cover only part of the consumer basket in some countries. The speech frames the evidence policymakers need to distinguish temporary price pressure from a broader shift in behaviour. It contains no recommendation for the next ECB rate decision (pp. 1–3).

How often firms reset prices matters because a shared increase in costs changes the incentive to wait. A firm may bring forward a price increase when its competitors face the same squeeze on margins. During the earlier inflation surge, research in the Eurosystem’s ChaMP network found that firms raised prices more frequently, with relatively little change in the size of individual increases. Italian survey evidence also suggests that upside surprises to input costs feed more strongly into selling prices than downside surprises. At the peak of the last episode, faster expected input-price growth accounted for about one-third of selling-price growth in the cited study. That estimate belongs to the earlier episode. The speech does not transplant it into today’s inflation forecast (p. 2).

Nicoletti Altimari identifies two cushions. Renewables generated half of EU electricity in 2025, 12 percentage points more than in 2021, weakening the link between gas and wholesale power prices in some markets. He assigns greater weight to demand. In 2021–22, reopening and fiscal transfers supported spending while supply chains remained strained. Energy-related fiscal measures averaged about 0.9% of euro-area GDP a year in 2022–24, against about 0.1% in 2026. In the present episode, low confidence, slower growth and easing demand for labour have limited firms’ ability to pass costs on. Wage pressure had yet to reaccelerate. Even so, producer prices for intermediate goods were 7.1% above a year earlier, leaving scope for delayed pass-through. Low-income households remain particularly exposed to energy and food, although limited food-price transmission had softened the disparity so far (pp. 2–4).

For bond investors, the source of tighter financial conditions matters as much as the rise in yields. Markets had anticipated further policy tightening after the ECB began raising rates in June, so expected policy was already restraining demand. Longer yields, especially in the United States, had risen more than expected short rates alone could explain. Possible explanations included higher expected productivity, increased compensation for inflationary supply shocks and concern over government borrowing. He found little quantitative evidence for another proposed driver, issuance by AI companies. Euro-area term premia also reflected US spillovers and renewed pressures in some sovereign markets. Most of the rise in corporate yields had come through higher benchmark rates, with credit spreads showing some pressure. Companies face the larger cash-flow effect as debts refinance (pp. 4–5).

A reversal in AI valuations could tighten conditions through a different mechanism. Concentrated exposures and arrangements in which suppliers and customers finance each other could transmit losses across balance sheets. Leverage and interconnected intermediaries could amplify a disorderly correction. The speaker presents a risk scenario without estimating its probability, its magnitude or the compensation available for bearing it (p. 5).

questions.question: Has the energy shock started changing the frequency of price increases outside energy?
questions.detail: The available microdata covered only some countries and products. The decisive signal for inflation persistence would be more widespread repricing alongside higher wage settlements and firmer demand. Compare the ChaMP micro-price evidence, harmonised consumer-price components, company pricing surveys and negotiated wages by country. The timing matters for whether the tightening already embedded in short rates will be sufficient.

questions.question: How much of higher long yields reflects expected monetary policy, and how much reflects compensation for duration or sovereign risk?
questions.detail: The speaker identifies several plausible channels but gives no quantitative decomposition. Compare overnight-indexed swap forwards and inflation expectations with term-premium estimates, sovereign spreads and auction data around comparable dates in the United States and euro area. If persistent term premia are doing much of the tightening, extending duration would expose investors to a different risk than a repricing of the ECB’s near-term path.

questions.question: Which firms would first transmit a refinancing or AI-valuation shock into real spending?
questions.detail: Benchmark rates explain much of the observed rise in corporate yields, while circular financing and leverage could distribute losses beyond AI issuers. Combine debt maturity schedules and fixed-rate shares with disclosed customer or supplier financing, collateral and counterparty concentrations. Company filings and financial-stability reports could identify exposures that the aggregate corporate spread misses.
